title: African buffalo
wiki_lead:
The African buffalo (Syncerus caffer) is a large bovine native to sub-Saharan Africa. First described in 1779 by Anders Sparrman, it is the only extant species of the genus Syncerus. Four subspecies are currently recognized: the Cape buffalo, West African savanna buffalo, Central African savanna buffalo, and African forest buffalo. It is a heavily built animal with a broad head and torso, a strong neck, large horns, and a bony armor or "boss" across the forehead of males. The fur ranges in color from rusty to black, and the tail ends with a dark, tuft of hair.
The African buffalo occurs in a variety of habitats, such as woodlands, savannas, forests, grasslands, shrublands, and wetlands. It is a ruminant and a grazer, primarily feeding on grass and dietary fiber. A social animal, the African buffalo forms herds ranging in size from a few individuals to over a thousand members. Herds typically consist of adult females and their young, and a number of adult males that temporarily join herds for mating opportunities. Males have a pecking order where dominant individuals hold the best access to mates. After a gestation of more than 10 months, females give birth to a single calf. Weaning occurs between 10 and 18 months, and the lifespan is about 12 years in the wild. Adult African buffaloes have few natural predators because of their size and aggression, though calves are much more vulnerable.
Since the 19th century, the African buffalo's range has greatly reduced due to human factors such as poaching, climate change, agriculture, and disease outbreaks. Despite this trend, conservation efforts have managed to increase populations in some parts of its range. As of 2019, it is listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List, with an estimated population of 398,000 to 401,000 mature individuals. A Big Five game animal, the African buffalo is legally hunted as a trophy in 16 out of 37 range countries. It has co-existed alongside humans for thousands of years and has in many ways contributed to human culture.

Taxonomy
The African buffalo was first described by Anders Sparrman as Bos caffer in 1779. Sparrman placed the species in the same genus (Bos) as the water buffalo, an animal described as Bos bubalis in 1758 by his mentor Carl Linnaeus. Later in the 19th century, the two species were placed into different genera, with the water buffalo being moved to Bubalus in 1827 by Charles Hamilton Smith and the African buffalo to Syncerus by Brian Hodgson in 1847. The genus Syncerus differs from Bos in the backwards-directed hairs along on the back of the neck, as well as in the lack of fusion between the palatine bone and the vomer in the roof of the mouth. Parallel evolution may explain the similar horn shapes in the two genera.
The African buffalo is a member of the Bovini tribe within the Bovinae subfamily of the Bovidae family. There are around 140 species within 40 genera in Bovidae; members are characterized by the presence of true horns in males or in both sexes. The Bovini tribe is further divided into three subtribes based on data of complete chromosome sets, and ribosomal and mitochondrial DNA sequences. Syncerus and Bubalus are placed in the Bubalina subtribe, that alongside the Bovina subtribe—which contains cattle, bison, yaks, gaurs, and bantengs—emerged 10–15 million years ago. Between 6 and 9.8 million years ago, Syncerus and Bubalus split from a common ancestor, according to genetic evidence. It is unclear which ancestor gave rise to the African buffalo but some hypotheses (which lack cladistic evidence) propose that Syncerus could be a direct descendent of the Pliocene bovid Simatherium which itself may have evolved from the earlier bovid Ugandax.

grok_lead: The African buffalo ( Syncerus caffer) is a robust bovid species endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, distinguished by its stocky build, dark coat, and characteristic bossâa thick, fused base where the horns emerge. It encompasses four subspecies: the Cape buffalo ( S. c. caffer), the largest and most iconic form found in southern and eastern savannas; the smaller forest buffalo ( S. c. nanus) adapted to rainforests; the West African savanna buffalo ( S. c. brachyceros); and the Central African savanna buffalo ( S. c. aequinoctialis). Adults typically measure 1.0 to 1.7 meters at the shoulder, with males weighing 500 to 900 kilograms, enabling them to traverse diverse habitats from floodplains and grasslands to woodlands and dense forests. African buffalo exhibit highly social behavior, forming stable herds led by females that can number from dozens to thousands, providing collective defense against predators such as lions and spotted hyenas through coordinated charges and horn displays. Their temperament is notoriously unpredictable and aggressive, particularly among solitary old males or when protecting calves, earning them a reputation as one of the continent's most perilous large mammals capable of charging at speeds up to 50 kilometers per hour without warning. Primarily grazers, they consume vast quantities of grass daily, influencing vegetation dynamics and supporting ecosystem health, though their preference for nutrient-rich floodplains exposes them to diseases like anthrax and corridor bottlenecks. Conservationally, the species is assessed as Near Threatened by the IUCN, with a global population estimated at around 400,000 individuals experiencing declines due to habitat loss, poaching, and disease outbreaks, disproportionately affecting rarer forest subspecies. As a key component of the "Big Five" in safari tourism, buffalo herds sustain predator populations and indicate grassland integrity, yet their management involves balancing human-wildlife conflict in expanding agricultural zones.
